response.title: I rent an apartment with its own gas furnace. Can I plug a portable battery in to keep the heat on during an outage?
response.answer:
Yes, you can potentially run your apartment's gas furnace from a portable battery power station during a power outage. In fact, gas furnaces are often good candidates for battery backup because the gas provides the heat—the electricity mainly runs the blower fan, ignition system, and controls.

However, there's one important catch: most residential gas furnaces are hardwired into the building's electrical system, not plugged into a wall outlet.

That means whether you can use a portable battery depends on how your furnace is connected.

1. How much battery power does a gas furnace need?

Typical estimates for a residential forced-air gas furnace:

Component

	

Power consumption




Blower fan

	

300–800 W




Ignition and controls

	

20–100 W




Startup surge

	

Can exceed 1,000 W




Total running power

	

Often 400–900 W

These figures vary significantly by furnace model. A modern variable-speed blower may consume much less electricity than an older blower motor.

For example, assuming your furnace draws 500 W while running:

Battery capacity

	

Approximate heating runtime*




1 kWh

	

1.7 hours




2 kWh

	

3.4 hours




3.6 kWh

	

6.1 hours




5 kWh

	

8.5 hours

These are cumulative furnace-running hours, assuming 85% usable AC energy. If the furnace runs only 50% of the time, the elapsed heating time could be roughly twice as long.

2. How to connect it safely

Option A: Furnace already has a plug

This is the easiest situation. If it has an approved standard power plug, you may be able to unplug it from the wall and connect it directly to a compatible portable power station.

Option B: Furnace is hardwired

A licensed electrician can install a compatible furnace transfer switch, with your landlord's approval. This isolates the furnace from utility power before connecting the battery. 
Reliance Controls
+1

Never connect the battery to a normal wall outlet to power the furnace circuit backward. Also, some furnaces require a particular neutral-ground configuration to ignite reliably, so compatibility needs checking before an outage.

3. Since you're renting

I'd recommend avoiding permanent modifications unless your landlord approves them. Before purchasing a battery, check how your furnace receives electricity.

Two questions:

Is your furnace in a closet inside your apartment, or in a garage/utility room?

Does it have a regular electrical plug going into an outlet, or do you see electrical wiring going directly into the furnace?

If you're not sure, you can send me a photo of the furnace and its electrical connections. I can help you identify which backup approach is practical and what size battery you'd need.
